questions.question: An interleaved schedule of T1 and T2 leaves the database in exactly the state that running T1 completely before T2 would have produced. What is this schedule called?
questions.explanation: A schedule is serializable when its outcome equals that of some serial ordering of its transactions, so the interleaving introduced no inconsistency.

questions.question: Schedules S1 and S2 start from the same database state and, despite ordering their operations differently, both end with A = 50 and B = 70. What equivalence do S1 and S2 have?
questions.explanation: Result equivalence compares only final database states — a weaker notion than conflict equivalence, which also requires identical ordering of all conflicting operations.

questions.question: S1 and S2 order every pair of conflicting operations — same data item, at least one of them a write — in exactly the same way, though non-conflicting pairs may differ. What equivalence do they have?
questions.explanation: Two schedules are conflict equivalent when all conflicting operation pairs appear in the same order; only non-conflicting pairs may be swapped between them.

questions.question: To test a schedule for conflict-serializability, you draw one node per transaction and a directed edge Ti → Tj whenever Ti's conflicting operation precedes Tj's. What is this graph called?
questions.explanation: The precedence (serialization) graph encodes the order of conflicting operations; the schedule is conflict-serializable exactly when the graph is acyclic.

questions.question: A 2PL variant releases exclusive locks only when the transaction commits, so no other transaction can ever read its uncommitted writes. Which variant is this?
questions.explanation: Strict 2PL holds write locks until commit, guaranteeing recoverable, cascadeless schedules; shared locks may still be released earlier, unlike the rigorous variant.

questions.question: A 2PL variant is even more restrictive: it holds both shared and exclusive locks until commit, eliminating the shrinking phase entirely. Which variant is this?
questions.explanation: Rigorous 2PL retains every lock — read and write — until commit, so transactions can be serialized in commit order and recoverability is automatic.

questions.question: Deadlock detection builds a directed graph with one node per active transaction and an edge Ti → Tj whenever Ti waits for a lock Tj holds; a cycle in it means deadlock. What is this structure?
questions.explanation: The wait-for graph captures 'is waiting for' edges between transactions; any cycle corresponds to a set of transactions blocked on one another forever.

questions.question: Under a timestamp-based deadlock prevention scheme, an older transaction may wait for a younger lock holder, but a younger requester is aborted and restarted instead of waiting. Which scheme is this?
questions.explanation: Wait-die is non-preemptive: only the requesting younger transaction 'dies', while an older requester simply waits — aborts flow old-to-young, preventing cycles.

questions.question: Under wound-wait, the younger transaction T2 (TS = 20) requests a lock currently held by the older transaction T1 (TS = 5). What happens to T2?
questions.explanation: Wound-wait lets an older requester abort a younger holder, but a younger requester may only wait for an older holder — so T2 blocks instead of preempting T1.

questions.question: Instead of locks, every transaction receives a timestamp, and any read or write that would violate the timestamp order is rejected, forcing the offending transaction to restart. Which concurrency protocol is this?
questions.explanation: Timestamp ordering serializes transactions by their assigned timestamps: older transactions must appear to run before younger ones, and out-of-order operations are rolled back.

questions.question: Building the precedence graph for schedule S yields edges T1 → T2, T2 → T3, and T3 → T1. What feature of the graph proves S is not conflict-serializable?
questions.explanation: Each edge forces one transaction to precede another in every equivalent serial order; the cycle T1→T2→T3→T1 demands each precede itself, so no serial order exists.

questions.question: Schedule: T1 reads A, T2 writes A, then T1 reads A again. Is this schedule conflict-serializable?
questions.explanation: The conflicts create edges T1->T2 and T2->T1, a cycle, so no equivalent serial order exists.

questions.question: Under timestamp ordering, transaction T (TS = 20) issues Write(X) where X was already written by a transaction with TS = 30. Rather than aborting T, the scheduler simply ignores the stale write. Which rule permits this?
questions.explanation: Thomas' Write Rule discards a write whose timestamp is older than the item's current write timestamp: the value is obsolete anyway, so skipping it preserves correctness without a restart.

questions.question: Transactions execute without taking locks; at commit time the system checks their read and write sets for conflicts against already-committed transactions and aborts the offender if found. Which concurrency method is this?
questions.explanation: OCC assumes conflicts are rare: transactions run in a read phase, are validated at commit, and restart only when validation fails — efficient when interference is uncommon.

questions.question: After a crash, recovery runs three passes — analysis rebuilds the transaction and dirty-page tables, redo repeats history to restore the exact pre-crash state, and undo removes the losers' effects. Which recovery algorithm is this?
questions.explanation: ARIES (Algorithms for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics) uses log sequence numbers and its analysis-redo-undo pipeline to recover while supporting fine-grained locking.

questions.question: Schedule S = R1(X); W2(X); W1(X); C1; C2. Build the precedence graph — is S conflict-serializable?
questions.explanation: R1(X) before W2(X) forces edge T1 -> T2, while W2(X) before W1(X) forces T2 -> T1; the cycle makes S non-conflict-serializable.

questions.question: Schedule S = R1(A); W1(A); R2(A); W2(B). The schedule is conflict-serializable — what is its equivalent serial order?
questions.explanation: The only conflict is W1(A) before R2(A), giving a single edge T1 -> T2; the precedence graph is acyclic with serial order T1, T2.

questions.question: Under basic timestamp ordering, transaction T with TS = 25 issues Read(X) while the write-timestamp of X is 30. What happens to T?
questions.answer: T is rolled back and restarted
alternatives: The read is rejected and T aborts
T is aborted and restarted with a new timestamp
questions.explanation: Reading X would expose a value written 'in the future' relative to T's timestamp, so the scheduler rejects the operation and restarts T.

questions.question: Under wound-wait deadlock prevention, older transaction T1 (TS = 5) requests a lock held by younger transaction T2 (TS = 20). What happens to T2?
questions.explanation: Wound-wait lets the older transaction preempt: the younger lock holder is aborted ('wounded') rather than being allowed to wait.

questions.question: T2 reads the value of X while T1's write is still uncommitted; T2 then commits while T1 is still active, and T1 subsequently aborts. Which schedule property did this violate?
questions.explanation: A recoverable schedule forbids a transaction from committing before every transaction whose writes it read; since T2 committed first, T1's abort would leave committed results built on undone data.
